content.leaderBio: Mr. Jigar Patel is the founder and Principal Officer of Neuron Wealth Advisors LLP, a SEBI-registered fee-only investment advisor. content.title: The people behind the advice

members.name: Dr. Hamsa Thota
members.bio: Founder and President of Innovation Business Development, Inc and board member of INSME. 35+ years of experience with 10 U.S. patents.
fullBio: Dr Hamsa Thota is the Founder and President of Innovation Business Development, Inc and currently serves on the board of the International Network for Small and Medium Enterprises (INSME). He is an advisor to the "Art of Science Learning Project", a US NSF funded R&D project to shape 21st-Century US workforce.

During his 35+ years of professional experience, he has developed and commercialized over 200 food products and holds 10 U.S. patents. He is a certified specialist in New Product Development and Organizational Engineering.

He has been a President and Chairman of the Product Development and Management Association (PDMA), USA. He served as an advisor to science and technology departments in China and is a frequent lecturer at national and international events on sustaining innovation, new product development, and the application of innovation best practice tools to grow business with profit.

He was a visiting professor at the Zhejiang University (China) and a guest lecturer at the University of Georgia for Marketing Research and Product Development courses. He co-authored “Key concepts in innovation”, a fundamental reference book on innovation for practitioners, students and scholars.

members.name: Mayank Patel
members.bio: CFA Charterholder and former CEO of CrAdLE with 20+ years in technology incubation, PE/VC investments, and strategic startup valuation.
fullBio: Mayank has more than twenty years of experience of working in technology business incubation, academics and banking & financial services sector. He is an Electrical Engineer, MBA (Finance) and a CFA Charterholder from CFA Institute, USA.

Mayank provides consulting for evaluation of start ups and for PE, VC and Startup Investments. He has been a CEO of EDII's technology business incubator, CrAdLE and mentored start-up for strategic financing, and business valuation. He has valued more than 100 small and medium enterprises for investment, especially for venture capital and private equity funding.

As a professor at various education institutions, he has taught students in various finance and investment management subjects including investment analysis, portfolio management, asset valuation, new enterprise financing, international finance and alternative investment.

members.name: Reecha Patel
members.bio: Practicing for 15+ years in taxation. Fellow member of ICAI, passed Uniform CPA exam (USA), with extensive experience in India & US tax compliance.

content.intro: Explaining the meaning of 'Association', one of the greatest Hindu monk, Swami Vivekananda ji said:
quoteLines: If it is caught in hands, it is pure enough for drinking.
If it falls in a gutter, its value drops so much that it can't be used even for washing the feet.
If it falls on a hot surface, it perishes.
If it falls on lotus leaf, it shines like a pearl and
finally, if it falls on an oyster, it becomes a pearl.
content.quoteConclusion: The drop is the same, but its existence & worth depend on with whom it associates.” Always be associated with people who are good at heart.

Regulation 15A of the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 governs fees and charging mechanisms, establishing fiduciary standards that protect both clients and advisers. NWA charges fees strictly on an advisory retainer or hourly basis, free of any product commissions, distribution incentives, or third-party kickbacks.
noLiabilityParagraphs: Investment advisory services provided by NWA represent professional guidance and financial stewardship based on asset allocation, research, and client risk tolerance.

Securities markets are subject to inherent market volatility, interest rate fluctuations, macroeconomic risks, and capital fluctuations. NWA does not guarantee any specific returns, capital preservation, or investment performance.
Accordingly, fees paid for advisory services are non-refundable on the grounds of investment portfolio performance, asset depreciation, or market downturns.
policyParagraphs: Advisory retainers are billed in advance on a quarterly, half-yearly, or annual basis as mutually agreed in the written Investment Advisory Agreement.

In the event of premature termination of advisory services by either the Client or the Investment Adviser, refunds shall be processed on a pro-rata basis for the unexpired portion of the billing period.

All refunds are calculated after deducting applicable statutory taxes, payment gateway or banking transaction charges, and statutory breakage fees for advisory work, onboarding, and comprehensive financial planning already executed.
content.procedureIntro: Our transparent 7-step procedure ensures compliant, auditable, and prompt processing of all eligible refund requests:

steps.title: Acknowledgment & Request Assessment

steps.title: Direct Client Verification

steps.title: Formal Determination
steps.description: The Investment Adviser shall notify the Client of the approval or rejection.

steps.title: Statutory Deductions & Breakage
steps.description: Refunds shall be made after deducting a cancellation fee for services already rendered or a breakage fee.

steps.title: Banking Channel Disbursement
steps.description: If the refund request is approved, the refund will be processed through banking channel either through cheque or through IMPS/NEFT/RTGS within 5 days.

steps.title: Bank Account Verification
steps.description: If the Client has not received a refund within 5 days of approval of refund, the Client is requested to check the bank account as it may take some time before the funds are available in the account.

steps.title: Escalation & Direct Assistance

timelineParagraphs: Approved refunds are disbursed within five (5) business days from the date of formal written approval.

Disbursements are made strictly to the Client's verified primary bank account via NEFT, RTGS, or IMPS banking channels to comply with PMLA (Prevention of Money Laundering Act) and SEBI anti-money laundering guidelines. Cash refunds or third-party bank disbursements are strictly prohibited.

content.heading: We Have Made This Journey Ourselves
paragraphs: Our founder, Jigar Patel, lived and worked in the United States for 9 years before moving back to India with his family.
He knows the numbers: the tax rules, the forms, the timing. He also knows the part nobody talks about: the emotions, the family expectations and the fear of getting a big decision wrong.
As a Chartered Accountant, US CPA and CFA charterholder, he and his team bring both sides of your financial life together in one plan.

content.heading: Your RNOR Years Are a Golden Window
content.leadText: When you first move back, you can usually qualify as Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR) for up to two or three years, depending on your years abroad and your move date. During this time:

sideImage.alt: Neuron Wealth Advisor discussing RNOR golden window transition with returning NRI client

points: Most income and gains from abroad are generally not taxed in India
Interest on FCNR deposits stays tax free
You do not need to report foreign assets in your Indian tax return
paragraphs: For many returning tech professionals who are not US citizens or Green Card holders, this window can be the most tax efficient time in their life to sell US shares, rebalance and decide what to keep abroad and what to bring to India. For US citizens and Green Card holders, the window works differently, and the plan must account for US tax too.
Used well, these years can protect a large part of your wealth. Used poorly, they simply pass by.
content.focusText: better returns after tax in India and the US, for the risk you are comfortable with, fully within Indian tax law, FEMA and US rules.

content.heading: Ten Decisions That Shape Your Wealth for Years

decisions.title: When to move
decisions.text: Your arrival date decides your tax status in India for years. A few weeks earlier or later can add or lose a full year of RNOR benefit.

decisions.title: Your last day, your vest dates and your move date
decisions.text: RSU vests, bonus payouts, ESPP purchases and severance should be lined up with your move. The wrong order can mean leaving money behind or paying tax twice.

decisions.title: Your RSUs and ESPP shares
decisions.text: RSUs that vest after you move may be taxed partly in the US and partly in India. We plan the timing, the foreign tax credit and the reporting, and decide which shares to hold or sell.

decisions.title: Concentrated stock in your employer
decisions.text: How much to keep, how much to sell, and when, so you diversify at the lowest possible tax across both countries.

decisions.title: Your 401(k), IRA and HSA
decisions.text: Keep, withdraw or roll over. Indian law offers relief that can align the tax on your US retirement accounts with the US timing, if you plan for it.

decisions.title: How much money to move, and when
decisions.text: Not everything needs to come to India at once. Some money is better kept abroad for a while. Some is better brought in early.

decisions.title: In whose name to move it
decisions.text: Your name, your spouse's or a joint account. The right choice can lower tax for the whole family.

decisions.title: How to move it
decisions.text: NRE, FCNR or RFC accounts, or a direct transfer. The right route protects your money from avoidable tax and currency costs.

decisions.title: Your US home and other US assets
decisions.text: Sell or rent your home, keep or close your US brokerage account. Some US brokers restrict accounts once you live abroad, and US shares held by non US persons carry US estate tax risk above a small limit.

decisions.title: Your new portfolio in India
decisions.text: A fresh investment plan for your new life, built for your goals, your risk comfort and your tax status in both countries, written into a clear Investment Policy Statement.

Still a good time. Most of the important decisions can be planned well.

steps.text: Fix your move date against your vest and bonus calendar. Review every account, share and retirement plan in the US. Decide what to sell, keep and move.

steps.text: Open the right accounts in India. Start moving money in a planned way. Finalise your 401(k), HSA and brokerage plan. Plan your final US tax year.
Convert NRE accounts to resident accounts, open RFC accounts where useful, update KYC and FEMA status. Put your new investment plan in place.
Use the tax window to diversify, sell foreign assets wisely and move money only when and where it makes sense.
An ongoing plan for your global wealth, with your Indian and US reporting handled correctly and reviewed every year.

content.heading: Small Decisions. Big Difference.
content.description: Moving home with your family is a big life decision. The smaller choices around it, like timing, names and amounts, often matter more than people expect. Planned well, they can help you:

points.text: Gain the full RNOR window by choosing the right move date
Keep more of your RSUs by lining up vesting, sales and foreign tax credits
Diversify a concentrated stock position at a lower tax cost
Keep your 401(k) working without surprise tax in India
Lower tax on your Indian income by structuring it across family members
Reduce currency costs by planning how and when money moves
Stay compliant in both countries with correct reporting and records

block2Items: US citizens continue to file US tax returns, wherever they live
Indian mutual funds are usually treated as PFIC in the US and can be complicated for novice investor or advisor
FBAR and FATCA reporting of your Indian accounts continues
Giving up a Green Card has its own rules and, for long term holders, a possible exit tax

content.block2Conclusion: We build your Indian portfolio so it works under both tax systems, and we work alongside your US CPA so both sides match.

content.block3Heading: A New Country Means a New Financial Plan
block3Paragraphs: Your taxes, investment options, expenses, income, goals and even your comfort with risk all change when you move. A plan made for life in California or Seattle will not work in Bengaluru, Hyderabad or Ahmedabad.
We rebuild your plan for your new life: your goals, your cash flow, your children's education, your parents' care and your retirement, with investments chosen for after tax returns in both countries.

faqs.q: When do I become a resident of India after I return?
faqs.a: Under FEMA, you become a resident when you return to live in India. For income tax, your status depends on the days you spend in India and your years abroad. Most returning NRIs are first RNOR, then fully resident.

faqs.q: What is RNOR and how long does it last?
faqs.a: RNOR means Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident. During this period most foreign income is generally not taxed in India. It usually lasts up to two or three years, depending on your years abroad and your move date.

faqs.q: How are my RSUs taxed if they vest after I move to India?
faqs.a: RSUs that vest after the move are often taxed partly in the US and partly in India, based on where you worked between grant and vesting. Credit for tax paid in one country can usually be claimed in the other. Planning the timing and the paperwork makes a big difference.

faqs.q: I am moving to my company's India office. What changes?
faqs.a: Your salary moves to Indian payroll, but your RSUs and ESPP usually stay in the US. Both countries may tax the same shares, and your employer may not handle it fully. We plan your transfer date, your vesting and your tax credits so you do not pay twice.

faqs.q: Can I keep my 401(k) and IRA after moving to India?
faqs.a: Yes, you can usually keep them. Indian tax law also offers relief that can align the tax on these accounts with US timing. Whether to keep, withdraw or roll over depends on your age, tax in both countries and your plans.

faqs.q: Should I sell my US shares before or after I move?
faqs.a: It depends on your citizenship, your visa status and your RNOR window. For some families, selling during the RNOR years is far more tax efficient. For US citizens and Green Card holders, US tax applies either way. We plan this share by share.

faqs.q: Can I keep my US brokerage account?
faqs.a: Often yes, but some US brokers restrict accounts once you live abroad. Also, US shares held by non US persons can carry US estate tax risk. We help you choose where and how to hold them.

faqs.q: What happens to my NRE and FCNR accounts?
faqs.a: NRE accounts must be converted to resident accounts once you return. FCNR deposits can continue until maturity, and their interest stays tax free while you are RNOR. You can also hold foreign currency in an RFC account.

faqs.q: I am a US citizen. Do I still file US taxes after moving?
faqs.a: Yes. US citizens file US tax returns wherever they live. With the DTAA and foreign tax credits, you can usually avoid paying tax twice, but it needs planning.

faqs.q: I have already moved back. Is it too late?
faqs.a: No. Many important decisions can still be made during your RNOR years. The earlier we start, the more options you have.

content.heading: You May Not Be an NRI Anymore
content.description: Many foreign citizens and OCI cardholders who have lived in India for years still think of themselves as NRIs. Under Indian law, they usually are not.
content.calloutQuote: Your passport does not decide your status. Where you live does.

laws.title: Under Indian income tax
laws.text: If you have lived in India long enough, you are a resident and usually an ordinary resident. India then taxes your global income, and you must report your foreign assets in your Indian tax return: bank accounts, investments, pensions, retirement accounts and property abroad.

laws.title: Under FEMA
laws.text: If you live in India to work or settle here, you are a resident. Your bank accounts, KYC and investments should reflect that. Holding NRE accounts or investing as an NRI when you are not one can create problems later.

content.warningBox: Missing this is common. The penalties for not reporting foreign assets in India can be heavy. The fix is simple once you know your status, and we help you get there quietly and correctly.

content.heading: Does Your Home Country Still Tax You?

cards.title: US citizens and Green Card holders
cards.text: The US taxes its citizens on their worldwide income, wherever they live. So you file a US tax return every year, and you also pay tax in India as a resident. Careful planning is essential to avoid paying twice.

cards.title: Citizens of most other countries
cards.text: The UK, Canada, Australia, Singapore and most other countries tax you mainly based on where you live. Once you are no longer resident there, they usually tax only income that comes from that country, such as rent, some pensions or gains on local property. But leaving properly matters. Some countries have strict tests for when you stop being resident, and some tax certain gains when you leave.

cards.title: For everyone
cards.text: India taxes your income from around the world once you are an ordinary resident. Your home country may tax part of the same income. The tax treaty between India and your country decides who taxes first and who gives credit.

content.heading: Tax Free in India Does Not Mean Tax Free at Home
content.introText: India and your home country can see the same income very differently. A few common examples:

examples.text: PPF and EPF interest, tax free bonds and some insurance maturity amounts are tax free in India, but may be taxed by your home country. For US citizens, they usually are.
Indian mutual funds are simple in India, but some countries tax them harshly. In the US they are usually treated as PFIC, with heavy tax and extra forms.
Section 80C savings reduce Indian tax but give no benefit abroad.
Pensions and retirement accounts abroad, like a 401(k), UK pension, RRSP or superannuation, may be treated very differently by India and by your home country.
Rent or gains on property back home may be taxed in both countries, with credit in one of them.

content.conclusionText: The result is simple. An investment that looks perfect in India can be a poor choice for a foreign citizen. Tax saving in India alone is not the goal.
content.conclusionHighlight: What matters is what you keep after tax in both countries.

sections.label: How Two Countries Share Your Tax

content.heading: How Two Countries Share Your Tax
content.description: India has tax treaties (DTAA) with most countries. Together with foreign tax credits, they are there to stop you paying tax twice. But they only work if you plan and file correctly.

rules.title: Who taxes first.
rules.text: For some income, India taxes first and your home country gives credit. For other income, it is the other way round. Getting this order wrong is the most common reason people pay tax twice.

rules.title: Different tax years.
rules.text: India runs April to March. The US runs January to December, the UK April to April and Australia July to June. Income and tax credits have to be matched across both, year after year.

rules.title: Credit in India for tax paid abroad.
rules.text: Tax paid in your home country on income from there can usually be claimed in India, with the correct form filed on time.

rules.title: Credit abroad for tax paid in India.
rules.text: Where your home country taxes the same income, it usually gives credit for Indian tax, if claimed correctly.

rules.title: Income that falls through the gap.
rules.text: Income that is tax free in one country has no tax to claim as credit in the other, so it can become a full cost unless it is planned.

content.footnote: Every treaty is different. This is where most families lose money without realising it, and where careful planning makes the biggest difference.

content.heading: Investing Abroad Is Possible. It Is Not Simple.
content.text: Before the first rupee leaves India, these rules come into play:

rules.title: How much you can send
rules.text: Under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), each resident individual can send up to a yearly limit abroad (currently USD 250,000). Each family member has their own limit, so planning across the family matters.

rules.title: TCS on what you send
rules.text: Tax is collected at source on many remittances above a threshold. It is not an extra tax, as it can be adjusted against your income tax or refunded, but it ties up your money until then. Planning who sends, when and for what purpose makes a real difference.

rules.title: What you can invest in
rules.text: FEMA allows most listed investments abroad, but some investments, like stakes in private companies, companies with links back to India, or certain structures, have extra rules. Money sent abroad and not used must be invested or brought back within a set time.

rules.title: How foreign income is taxed in India
rules.text: Foreign dividends, interest and capital gains are taxed in India, often differently from Indian investments. Holding periods, tax rates and rules are not the same.

rules.title: Foreign tax credit
rules.text: Tax deducted abroad, like US tax on dividends, can usually be claimed as credit in India under the tax treaty (DTAA), but only if the right form is filed on time.

rules.title: Reporting foreign assets
rules.text: Every foreign account, share, fund and property must be reported in your Indian tax return, on a calendar year basis. Penalties for missing this can be heavy, even if no income was earned.

rules.title: Gifts to family abroad
rules.text: FEMA's list of relatives you can gift to is narrower than the list under income tax. A gift that is tax free in India may still not be allowed under FEMA, and it may need reporting in your child's country.

rules.title: US estate tax
rules.text: If you hold US shares or US based funds directly, your family may face US estate tax on them after your death, above a small limit, even though you have never lived in the US. This is one of the most overlooked risks for Indian investors.

faqs.q: How much money can I invest abroad from India?
faqs.a: Each resident individual can send money abroad up to the yearly limit under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (currently USD 250,000). Each family member has their own limit. Families investing through companies or trusts follow different rules.

faqs.q: Is TCS on foreign remittance an extra tax?
faqs.a: No. TCS collected on your remittance can be adjusted against your income tax or claimed as a refund. But it ties up your money until then, so it is worth planning.

faqs.q: How are my foreign investments taxed in India?
faqs.a: As a resident, your foreign dividends, interest and gains are taxed in India. Tax deducted abroad can usually be claimed as foreign tax credit under the tax treaty, with the right form filed on time.

faqs.q: Do I need to report my foreign investments in India?
faqs.a: Yes. Every foreign account, investment and property must be reported in your Indian tax return, even if it earned no income in the year.

faqs.q: What is US estate tax and does it affect me?
faqs.a: If you hold US shares or US based funds directly, they may be subject to US estate tax after your death, above a small limit, even if you have never lived in the US. The right fund choice and structure can reduce this risk.

faqs.q: Should I invest through GIFT City?
faqs.a: GIFT City offers dollar investments through an Indian regulated platform, and can suit many families. But products vary widely in cost, tax, liquidity and holdings. We review each option against your goals before you invest.

faqs.q: Can you manage my Interactive Brokers account?
faqs.a: We are registered as an adviser on Interactive Brokers. Your account stays in your name. We advise you on your global portfolio, help you implement it and monitor it regularly.

faqs.q: Can I gift money to my child living abroad?
faqs.a: Yes, within the LRS limit and to relatives as defined under FEMA. Your child may need to report it in their country. We plan gifts so they work under FEMA, Indian tax and the rules where your child lives.

faqs.q: Can I buy property abroad?
faqs.a: Yes, within the LRS limit. How you pay for it, rent it, report it and later sell it all have rules in India and abroad. We help you plan it across family members and years.

paragraphs: The investment value depends on the performance of the companies or mutual fund or security invested and its prospects. paragraphs: Price risk is the risk of increase / decrease in the value of a security or an investment portfolio without change in the fundamentals or value of investments. Investment advisor will employ a number of tools and techniques to manage price risk, ranging from relatively conservative decisions to aggressive strategies and balancing it with diversified portfolio.

functions.title: Liquidity Risk
paragraphs: Liquidity risk occurs when an investment cannot be converted into cash immediately without any effect on the price. The Investment Advisor tries to mitigate the risks by investing in securities based on the liquidity requirement of the client.

functions.title: Service Provider Risk
paragraphs: Investment Advisor is reliant upon the performance of third-party service providers for some functions e.g. research, reporting, etc.. functions.title: Credit Risk
paragraphs: Credit risk is the probability of a financial loss resulting from an organization’s failure to repay the loan or redeem the investment. Investment Advisor mitigates credit risk by analyzing the fund’s/borrower's creditworthiness/ investments, such as their current debt load and income, ratings of the funds and recommend investing in the securities that is suitable to the investor.

functions.title: Interest Rate Risk
paragraphs: Interest rate risk is the risk that an investment's value will change as a result of a change in interest rates. This risk affects the value of bonds/debt instruments more directly than stocks. Any reduction in interest rates will increase the value of the instrument and vice versa. Investment Advisor endeavors to consider the interest rate risks while recommending investments that is suitable to the investor.

functions.title: Reinvestment Risk
paragraphs: Reinvestment risk is the chance that cash flows received from an investment will earn less when put to use in a new investment. Investment Advisor attempts to recommend investments considering the financial goals of the investor so the reinvestment risk can be minimized.

functions.title: Currency Risk
paragraphs: Investors having investments across multiple countries or investors from out of India investing in India are exposed to currency risk that may create unpredictable profits and losses in their local currency. Investment Advisors endeavors to considers currency risk for such investors while evaluating suitability of investment.

content.directiveTitle: In accordance with the third schedule of IA Regulations u/r 15(9) of the IA Regulations which covers the Code of conduct for investment adviser:
content.directiveText: Neuron Wealth Advisors LLP strictly abides by all statutory standards of integrity, professional skill, thorough analysis, client confidentiality, and fair dealing established by the Securities and Exchange Board of India.

principles.title: Honesty and fairness
principles.statement: An investment adviser shall act honestly, fairly and in the best interests of its clients and in the integrity of the market.

principles.title: Diligence
principles.statement: An investment adviser shall act with due skill, care and diligence in the best interests of its clients and shall ensure that its advice is offered after thorough analysis and taking into account available alternatives.

principles.title: Capabilities
principles.statement: An investment adviser shall have and employ effectively appropriate resources and procedures which are needed for the efficient performance of its business activities.

principles.title: Information about clients
principles.statement: An investment adviser shall seek from its clients, information about their financial situation, investment experience and investment objectives relevant to the services to be provided and maintain confidentiality of such information.

principles.title: Information to its clients
principles.statement: An investment adviser shall make adequate disclosures of relevant material information while dealing with its clients.

principles.title: Fair and reasonable charges
principles.statement: An investment adviser advising a client may charge fees, subject to any ceiling as may be specified by the Board. The investment adviser shall ensure that fees charged to the clients is fair and reasonable.

principles.title: Conflicts of interest
principles.statement: An investment adviser shall try to avoid conflicts of interest as far as possible and when they cannot be avoided, it shall ensure that appropriate disclosures are made to the clients and that the clients are fairly treated.

principles.title: Compliance
principles.statement: An investment adviser including its partners, principal officer and persons associated with investment advice, as the case may be, shall comply with all regulatory requirements applicable to the conduct of its business activities so as to promote the best interests of clients and the integrity of the market.

principles.title: Responsibility of senior management
principles.statement: The senior management of the LLP shall bear primary responsibility for ensuring the maintenance of appropriate standards of conduct and adherence to proper procedures by the LLP.

dosItems.text: Always deal with SEBI registered Investment Advisers.

Always ask for your risk profiling before accepting investment advice. Insist that Investment Adviser provides advisory strictly on the basis of your risk profiling and take into account available investment alternatives.
Ask all relevant questions and clear your doubts with your Investment Adviser before acting on advice.
Assess the risk–return profile of the investment as well as the liquidity and safety aspects before making investments.

Don’t take decisions just because of repeated messages and calls by Investment Advisers.
Do not fall prey to limited period discount or other incentive, gifts, etc. offered by Investment advisers.
Don’t rush into making investments that do not match your risk taking appetite and investment goals.
Do not share login credential and password of your trading, demat or bank accounts with the Investment Adviser.

content.preambleTitle: Functions, obligations, duties and responsibilities of the Investment Adviser (including principal officer and all persons associated with the investment advice) include the following, subject to this agreement:

functions.title: Fiduciary duty
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall act in a fiduciary capacity towards its clients and shall disclose all conflicts of interests as and when they arise.

functions.title: Restricted Consideration
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall not receive any consideration by way of remuneration or compensation or in any other form from any person other than the client being advised, in respect of the underlying products or securities for which advice is provided.

functions.title: Arms-Length activities
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall maintain an arms-length relationship between its activities as an investment adviser and other activities.

functions.title: Segregation of IA services
paragraphs: The investment adviser which is also engaged in activities other than investment advisory services shall ensure that the investment advisory services are clearly segregated from all other activities, in the manner as prescribed under the IA Regulations.

functions.title: Disclosure of conflict of interest
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall ensure that in case of any conflict of interest of the investment advisory activities with other activities, such conflict of interest shall be disclosed to the client.

functions.title: Non-disclosure of confidential information
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall not divulge any confidential information about its clients, which has come to its knowledge, without taking prior permission of its clients, except where such disclosures are required to be made in compliance with any law for the time being in force.

However, the client hereby agree, acknowledge, consent and permit to the processing and use of the confidential information including personal data and financial data, by the adviser including third party vendors, as far as it is necessary for the performance of functions, obligations and responsibilities, towards providing services, herein.

The Client also agrees and allows the Adviser to include a general description of work performed for the purpose of demonstrating its experience to other potential clients or prepare and share it as a case study or use any other mode without naming the Client. The Adviser will also be entitled to use the Client as a reference to other potential work or clients.

functions.title: Restricted Transactions contrary to advise given
paragraphs: The investment advisor shall not enter into transactions on its own account which is contrary to its advice given to the client for a period of fifteen days from the day of such advice.

Provided that during the period of such fifteen days, if the investment adviser is of the opinion that the situation has changed, then it may enter into such a transaction on its own account after giving such revised assessment to the client at least 24 hours in advance of entering into such transaction.

The client agrees that the advice given is subject to a specific set of factors including the client-profile, risk-profile, goals, market conditions and others, and such set of factors differ for different persons including the adviser. Therefore, the client agrees to consent and permit that the investment adviser may enter into transactions on its own account which may be contrary to the advice given to the client. In case, the client need any confirmation or clarification or have any objection in investment adviser’s such transactions or holding or position, the client shall notify the adviser immediately.

functions.title: KYC compliance
paragraphs: The investment advisor shall follow Know Your Client (‘KYC’) procedure as specified by the Board from time to time.

functions.title: Code of Conduct
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall abide by Code of Conduct as specified in Third Schedule of the IA Regulations – contained as in Schedule G.

functions.title: Restricted Transactions on own account
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall not act on its own account, knowingly to sell securities or investment products to or purchase securities or investment product from a client.

functions.title: Prior approval for change in control
paragraphs: In case of change in control of the investment adviser, prior approval from the Board shall be taken.

functions.title: Submission of Information
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall furnish to the Board, information and reports as may be specified by the Board from time to time.

functions.title: Compliance with Certification and Qualification requirements
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall ensure compliance with the certification and qualification requirements as specified u/r 7 of IA Regulations, at all times.
These include, the qualification and certification requirement for a principal officer and for the persons associated with investment advice.

functions.title: Compliance with Regulatory mandates
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall ensure compliance with the Regulatory mandates.

functions.title: Compliance with Eligibility criteria
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall ensure compliance with the eligibility criteria as specified under the IA Regulations at all times.

functions.title: Risk profiling and suitability
paragraphs: The investment adviser follows a set process of risk profiling, risk assessment and suitability analysis, as mandated u/r 16 and 17 of IA Regulations and other regulatory mandates, including risk capacity and risk aversion.

functions.title: Reports to clients
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall provide reports to the client on potential and current investments, as required.

functions.title: Maintenance of records
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall maintain the records, as specified u/r 19(1) of IA Regulations and related books of accounts including client accounts and data.

functions.title: Audit as per the IA Regulations
paragraphs: The investment adviser shall conduct yearly audit u/r 19(3) of IA Regulations, in respect of compliance with the IA Regulations.

content.ethicsIntro: Members of CFA Institute (including CFA charterholders) and candidates for the CFA designation must adhere to the following principles:

ethics.title: Integrity, Competence & Respect
ethics.desc: Act with integrity, competence, diligence, respect and in an ethical manner with the public, clients, prospective clients, employers, employees, colleagues in the investment profession, and other participants in the global capital markets.

ethics.title: Client & Profession Supremacy
ethics.desc: Place the integrity of the investment profession and the interests of clients above their own personal interests.

ethics.title: Reasonable Care & Independent Judgment
ethics.desc: Use reasonable care and exercise independent professional judgment when conducting investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment actions, and engaging in other professional activities.

ethics.title: Exemplary Ethical Leadership
ethics.desc: Practice and encourage others to practice in a professional and ethical manner that will reflect credit on themselves and the profession.

ethics.title: Capital Markets Integrity
ethics.desc: Promote the integrity and viability of the global capital markets for the ultimate benefit of society.

ethics.title: Continuous Professional Excellence
ethics.desc: Maintain and improve their professional competence and strive to maintain and improve the competence of other investment professionals.

content.standardsTitle: Standards of Professional Conduct (Standards I – VII)
content.standardsText: Detailed statutory rules governing fiduciary relationships, professional independence, fair dealing, and conflict management.

substandards.name: Knowledge of the Law
substandards.desc: Understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the Code and Standards) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing professional activities. In the event of conflict, comply with the stricter law, rule, or regulation. Never knowingly participate or assist in violations.

substandards.name: Independence and Objectivity
substandards.desc: Use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in professional activities. Do not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that could compromise independence and objectivity.

substandards.name: Misrepresentation
substandards.desc: Do not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities.

substandards.name: Misconduct
substandards.desc: Do not engage in any professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit or commit any act that reflects adversely on professional reputation, integrity, or competence.

substandards.name: Material Nonpublic Information
substandards.desc: Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information.

substandards.name: Market Manipulation
substandards.desc: Do not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants.

substandards.name: Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
substandards.desc: Duty of loyalty to clients; act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment. Act for the benefit of clients and place clients’ interests before employer’s or own personal interests.

substandards.name: Fair Dealing
substandards.desc: Deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities.

substandards.name: Suitability
substandards.desc: Make reasonable inquiry into client's investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial constraints prior to making recommendations; judge suitability of investments in the context of the client’s total portfolio.

substandards.name: Performance Presentation
substandards.desc: When communicating investment performance information, make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete.

substandards.name: Preservation of Confidentiality
substandards.desc: Keep information about current, former, and prospective clients strictly confidential unless the information concerns illegal activities, disclosure is required by law, or client permits disclosure.

substandards.name: Loyalty
substandards.desc: Act for the benefit of employer and do not deprive employer of the advantage of skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm.

substandards.name: Additional Compensation Arrangements
substandards.desc: Do not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or creates a conflict of interest with employer’s interest without written consent from all parties.

substandards.name: Responsibilities of Supervisors
substandards.desc: Make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to supervision complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards.

substandards.name: Diligence and Reasonable Basis
substandards.desc: Exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investments, making recommendations, and taking investment actions supported by adequate research and investigation.

substandards.name: Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
substandards.desc: Disclose the basic format and general principles of investment processes; disclose significant limitations and risks; distinguish between fact and opinion in presentations.

substandards.name: Record Retention
substandards.desc: Develop and maintain appropriate records to support investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and all other investment-related communications.

substandards.name: Disclosure of Conflicts
substandards.desc: Full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to clients, prospective clients, and employer.

substandards.name: Priority of Transactions
substandards.desc: Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner.

substandards.name: Referral Fees
substandards.desc: Disclose to employer, clients, and prospective clients any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from, or paid to, others for the recommendation of products or services.

standards.title: Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate

substandards.name: Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
substandards.desc: Do not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs.

substandards.name: Reference to CFA Institute, Designation, and Program
substandards.desc: Do not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program.
